clue.text: A smooth king I joined for relaxing stretch after runs

indicators.note: Things joined are set end to end in the order given, so each piece named simply follows the one before it.

parts.note: the clue's opening word, taken as the single letter it already is
to press a shirt is to smooth it flat under an iron
K is the king in chess notation and on a playing card
the pronoun stands for itself, one letter

explanation.surface: Teaming up with an unruffled monarch for a rest after a spot of running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' reads as jogging and means the pistes, while 'smooth' reads as the king's manner and is the verb for what an iron does to cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Apres-ski is the drinking and lounging that follows a day on the slopes, so the runs are ski runs and the stretch is what comes after them.

clue.text: Storm increased? Ensure operation of watch

parts.note: the loudest part of a storm is its blowing, and weather talk swaps the two words freely
prices, numbers and volumes that have increased are all said to be up

explanation.surface: A weather bulletin warning the gale has strengthened, and a reminder to check your watch works.
explanation.walkthrough: A mechanical watch runs only while its mainspring is tight, so the definition is the whole phrase about keeping it going, not the single word 'watch'.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind up a watch is to turn the crown and tighten the spring that drives the hands, which is precisely ensuring it will run.

clue.text: Guidance on tempo, contemporary inspiration for poets

parts.note: a mod is somebody bang up to the minute; the word is clipped from modern and British youth of the 1960s wore it as a name
Erato is the Greek muse of lyric poetry, one of the nine sisters a poet was supposed to call on

explanation.surface: A shopping list for a young writer: advice on rhythm and a thoroughly up-to-date muse.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine Muses are permanent crossword furniture — Erato for love poetry, Clio for history, Terpsichore for dance — and their names repay learning by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Moderato is the Italian word written into a score telling the player to hold a middling speed, which is guidance on tempo.

clue.text: Spell as part of school learning

definitions.meaning: the noun meaning a stretch of time — a spell of fine weather, a spell in office
the named slot on a timetable in which one subject is taught

explanation.surface: Learning to spell, presented as one of the things schoolchildren do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' reads as the classroom business of s-p-e-l-l-i-n-g, which is what the mention of school is there to encourage, and the sense wanted is the time one.
explanation.definitionFit: A period is a spell of time, and it is also the block of the school day given over to a single lesson.

clue.text: Old man's at home, thus visits for little while

parts.note: 'pop' is the familiar word for a father, and the apostrophe-s comes along as the fourth letter
somebody at home is in, the everyday sense rather than any instruction

explanation.surface: Father is at home, so he calls round on people for a short stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At home' is where a solver expects a container instruction, since 'in' usually means something goes inside something else, and here it is only a two-letter synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To pop in is to call on somebody briefly and be gone again, so the phrase means visiting for no more than a little while.

clue.text: Minister in bygone days supported by some troops

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever supports a thing sits underneath it, so the letters named afterwards go below the ones already found.

parts.note: bygone days are the past, one phrase for the other
OR is Other Ranks, the British Army's term for the soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: A government minister of former times propped up by a section of the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks political, especially with troops standing behind him, and the word wanted is the church one — a fine piece of misdirection from a two-word charade.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastor is the minister of a congregation, the person who leads its worship, so this is a plain synonym in the ecclesiastical sense.

clue.text: Recovery vehicles? Some have clocks

definitions.note: The second definition describes rather than substitutes: it says what some of these things carry, which is how a setter defines a thing too plain to have a synonym.
definitions.meaning: the question mark flags a coined agent noun: things that do the towing when a car breaks down
the tall stone kind, and the ones on churches and town halls carry a public face and hands

explanation.surface: A question about breakdown trucks and which of them come fitted with clocks.
explanation.walkthrough: Anything that tows can be called a tower, which is what the question mark apologises for; the second reading has left vehicles behind entirely and gone to architecture.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the agent noun from 'tow', the trucks that haul wrecks away; the other is the building, and many carry a public clock.

clue.text: Piece of crossword that's out of date

definitions.meaning: a grid is ruled into these, one per letter
the slang sense: conventional, unhip, behind the times

explanation.surface: A single cell of a crossword grid, dismissed as old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: Calling a person square — dull, conformist, hopelessly behind the fashion — is 1950s jazz slang that has survived in crosswords long after it left the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword grid is ruled into squares, so the first definition names one cell; the second is the old slang for somebody unfashionable.

clue.text: Left supporter for very brief moment

parts.note: to split is to leave in a hurry, 1960s slang whose past tense is the same word
to second a motion is to back it, so the backer is a second — as is the boxer in the corner

explanation.surface: Somebody who backed the political left, and then only for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' wants to be the political wing, especially sitting next to 'supporter', and it is the past tense of a verb meaning departed.
explanation.definitionFit: A split second is the smallest slice of time anyone bothers to name, a second cut into pieces, so it is a very brief moment indeed.

clue.text: Climb in a second, somehow dropping nothing

indicators.note: 'Somehow' means by an unspecified route, so the letters beside it arrive in an order nobody promised.
What is dropped falls out and never arrives, so the letter named here leaves the material before it is rearranged.

parts.note: seven letters of raw material, the article and the unit of time together
'nothing' is the letter O, which comes out of that material first

explanation.surface: Someone about to start climbing in a second, and not dropping a thing on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' as the letter O is the crossword's most-used piece of shorthand — zero drawn as a ring — and here it goes before any shuffling happens.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to move upward under your own effort, so 'climb' is a verb-for-verb synonym in its ordinary intransitive sense.

clue.text: Affected as minutes may be

definitions.note: The second definition is a frame rather than a synonym: it hands you the sentence 'minutes may be —' and leaves you to complete it.
definitions.meaning: the adjective for someone mincing and over-refined in manner
the everyday sense: highly valued, especially when there are few left

explanation.walkthrough: The affected sense — a precious little man, all airs and delicacy — is the harder of the two, and the theme of this grid makes the minutes reading the easier one.
explanation.definitionFit: Precious covers both a mannered, over-refined person and anything highly valued, which is what minutes become when they are running out.

clue.text: Lots of the past one's misrepresented

indicators.note: Something misrepresented has been put across the wrong way round, so the letters beside it come out in the wrong order.

parts.note: four letters of raw material, the word and its apostrophe-s together

explanation.surface: A version of history that somebody has told wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is fodder, not grammar — a favourite setter's trick, because 'one's' looks like a possessive rather than four letters waiting to be moved.
explanation.definitionFit: Eons are immense stretches of elapsed time, so 'lots of the past' names them by sheer quantity rather than by any event in them.

clue.text: Two-times quiet husband one defames first off

indicators.note: 'First off' takes the front letter away from the word beside it and leaves the remainder standing.

parts.note: P is piano in a score, the composer's mark for playing quietly
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, as on a form
the Roman numeral for one
to defame somebody is to slander them, and the S at the front is what walks off

explanation.surface: A mild, quiet husband whose name somebody is busy blackening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two-times' looks like arithmetic at the head of the clue and is the verb for cheating on a partner, which leaves the rest of the sentence as four pieces in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: To philander is to carry on flirtations and affairs behind a partner's back, which is exactly what two-timing somebody means.

clue.text: Saying there's no difference between porridge and bread

parts.note: doing porridge is British slang for serving a prison sentence, after the oatmeal that was the old jail breakfast
declaring two things no different is declaring one to be the other, and that is the little verb in the middle
bread is long-standing slang for cash, the same joke as dough

explanation.surface: A claim that prison porridge and a slice of bread amount to much the same thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge and bread look like a grumble about stodgy food, and each is doing slang duty instead — one for a jail term, one for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the proverb that hours spent are money earned or lost, so 'Saying' defines it by class rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Send up kind of person to begin with that can help one cook breakfast

definitions.text: that can help one cook breakfast

indicators.note: In a down clue 'up' means reading back up the column, so the word beside it is entered the other way about.
'To begin with' puts the piece it follows at the very front, before anything else is added.

parts.note: a good egg is an old-fashioned way of calling somebody a decent sort, so an egg here is a person
to send money is to remit it, and this down clue stands that word on its head

explanation.surface: A send-up of the sort of person who will help you get breakfast cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send up' looks like a single phrase meaning to mock, and the setter is using its two words separately. The person who turns out to be an egg is the other stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg timer is the little sand glass that tells you when a boiled egg is done, so it earns its keep at the breakfast table.

clue.text: Is dividing lyric poems — they're presented on separate occasions

indicators.note: What divides a thing goes into the middle of it and pushes the halves apart, which is where these two letters land.

parts.note: an epode is a Greek lyric form, a short line answering a long one
the little verb is taken at face value, two letters lifted straight out of the clue

explanation.surface: A remark that some lyric poems are being split up and performed on different nights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is not doing grammar here but supplying letters, and 'lyric poems' points at a Greek form most solvers only ever meet in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Episodes are the separate instalments of a serial, each shown or published on its own occasion, so the definition describes them by how they arrive.

clue.text: Extremely small fraction of hour

definitions.meaning: the adjective for something tiny enough to need a lens
the noun: one sixtieth of one

explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions run together into a single phrase, which is the trap. They are pronounced differently too — my-NEWT for the tiny sense, MIN-it for the sixty seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute is both the adjective meaning tiny and the noun for a sixtieth of an hour: one spelling doing duty for two quite separate words.

clue.text: Reported with minimal impact in periodical

indicators.note: Something reported reaches you by ear, so what counts about the words beside it is the noise they make, not their spelling.

parts.note: something done with minimal impact is done feebly, and that adverb said aloud can be written a second way

explanation.surface: A story that made the papers but barely left a mark on anybody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodical' is the definition and also the word holding the surface up, since a report appearing in a magazine is exactly what the sentence appears to describe.
explanation.definitionFit: A weekly is a magazine or newspaper that comes out every seven days, so 'periodical' names it by class: a publication appearing at fixed intervals.

clue.text: Starts off by installing one sensible kind of clock

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition is a noun phrase: it names the compound the answer belongs to rather than offering a word you could swap in.

indicators.note: 'Starts off' asks for the letters the following words start off with, one from the front of each.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the three words, taken in order
a sensible decision is a logical one, straight synonym

explanation.surface: A workman who begins the job by putting in one sensible sort of clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The clock meant is the body's own, the internal rhythm that decides when you feel sleepy, and not a thing anybody could install.
explanation.definitionFit: The body's built-in cycle of sleeping and waking is called the biological clock, so the definition points at the word that qualifies it.

clue.text: Recluse concealing a source of something for days or more

definitions.text: source of something for days or more

indicators.note: What conceals a thing closes around it, so the letter named next is hidden inside the word before it.

parts.note: a recluse keeps away from company, which is what this word for a solitary sort means
the clue's own indefinite article, one letter taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A hermit keeping quiet about where something he has had for days came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A source of something for days or more' is a roundabout way of naming whoever lends you a thing — the garage that hands you a car while yours is being fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: A loaner is one who loans, so it is the source of whatever you have been given the use of for days or longer.

clue.text: Part of clock I never restrict the movement of

indicators.note: 'Part of' says the answer is a piece of what follows, sitting there already and in order.

parts.note: six consecutive letters, beginning one letter into the first word and running through the next two

explanation.surface: A component of a clock whose movement the speaker says they never restrict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' does double work: it is the horologist's word for the works of a clock, which is what the surface leans on, and the definition wants the plain sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To lock something in is to fasten it so it cannot shift, which is restricting its movement exactly.

clue.text: Broadcast time for piece of news

indicators.note: Broadcasting is the farmer's word for scattering seed by hand, so what it touches lands in no particular order.

parts.note: four letters of raw material, the word taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A bulletin going out on air at the slot booked for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast time' reads as the hour a programme is scheduled to go out, and the two words are really an instruction and the material it works on.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is one of the separate stories read out in a news bulletin, so 'piece of news' defines it in the newsroom's own sense.

clue.text: Apply pressure about ten to three, say? As long as it takes

definitions.note: The definition is an adverbial phrase and the answer a noun, which the idiom licenses: 'for the duration' and 'for as long as it takes' say the same thing.

indicators.note: Something placed about another goes right round it, so the first letters found here wrap themselves around the ones that follow.

parts.note: to dun a debtor is to keep pressing them for payment, an old word crosswords have kept alive
ten to three is a proportion of the sort written with a colon, and 'say' marks it as one example of the kind

explanation.surface: Somebody leaning on a debtor at around ten to three in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ten to three' is a clock time in the surface and a proportion in the wordplay, and the question mark is the setter's signal that it is only one instance of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Duration is how long something lasts, and 'as long as it takes' is the idiom for the same span: whatever amount of time the job needs.

clue.text: Records hits

definitions.meaning: the verb for registering a speed on a dial: the radar recorded him at ninety
British informal, the verb for landing a punch on somebody

explanation.surface: A list of chart-topping records.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like the music business, records and hits sitting side by side, and both are verbs here — one for measuring a speed, one for throwing a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: To clock a speed is to register it on a dial, and to clock somebody, in British slang, is to thump them; both are third-person verbs.

clue.text: Team's schedule for tea-break

definitions.note: The second definition is loose: the answer is the hour a mid-morning break is scheduled for rather than a schedule itself.
definitions.meaning: in cricket and football a side is named for the number of players it puts out
elevenses is the British mid-morning pause for tea and a biscuit, named after the hour it happens at

explanation.surface: A sports side's fixture list, worked out around when they stop for tea.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket or football side is an eleven because that is how many take the field, and elevenses is the British break taken at that hour — two senses of one number.
explanation.definitionFit: An eleven is a full cricket or football side, and eleven o'clock is the hour Britain sets aside for its mid-morning tea break.

clue.text: Tiny fellow, see, is punctual

parts.note: Tiny Tim is the small boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol, so a tiny fellow hands over his name
a see is the district a bishop governs, and Ely is the cathedral city in Cambridgeshire that heads one

explanation.surface: A remark that the little chap, you see, always turns up on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the crossword's standing request for a bishop's seat, and the short English ones — Ely, Wells, Ripon — are the ones worth knowing by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Something timely arrives at the right moment, which is what punctual means, though timely stretches further to cover anything opportune.
